The Green catbird Ailuroedus crassirostris exhibits a suite of reproductive traits typical of many Australasian passerines. The eggs themselves are substantial, measuring 4.1 centimeters in length and 2.7 centimeters in width, which yields a calculated fresh egg mass of approximately 15.6 grams.

Neonatal body mass at the moment of hatching is remarkably modest given the eventual size of the adult. Newly hatched Green catbird chicks weigh approximately 13 grams [Wwb = approximately 13 grams], a value that underscores their altricial state of development; they are initially blind, nearly naked, and entirely dependent on parental provisioning for thermoregulation and nutrition. This birth mass stands in stark contrast to the ultimate wet weight attained by adults, which averages 180 grams [Wwi = 180 grams], though considerable intraspecific variation exists. The nestlings undergo rapid feather development and muscle growth, achieving their first sustained flight and departing the nest at 21 days after hatching [tx = 21 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This fledging period, though brief, demands intensive biparental care to support the energetic cost of tissue synthesis and thermoregulation. Following nest departure, the fledglings remain dependent on adult provisioning for several additional weeks as they refine their foraging skills. The subsequent transition to gonadal maturity occurs more gradually; puberty is attained at 63 days after hatching [tp = 63 days after hatching], a relatively protracted interval for a passerine of this body size, which may be linked to the need to complete skeletal growth and accumulate sufficient lipid reserves before engaging in the demanding courtship and nesting behaviors typical of the species at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C].

At the same thermal baseline of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] that characterizes their active metabolic state, the maximum recorded lifespan for this species reaches approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years]. This longevity is notable for a medium-sized passerine and suggests a relatively slow life-history pace, with sustained adult survival compensating for the modest annual reproductive output of a single clutch.

Beyond its life-history parameters, the Green catbird occupies a distinctive ecological niche within the rainforests of eastern Australia, where it serves as a key frugivore and seed disperser for a variety of native fig species and other fleshy-fruited plants. Its vocal behavior is similarly distinctive; the species is renowned for its varied and often mimetic song, which incorporates calls of other bird species and even mechanical sounds from the environment, a trait it shares with its close relatives in the genus Ailuroedus. Comparative analyses with other members of the Ptilonorhynchidae, the bowerbird family to which it belongs, reveal that the Green catbird's relatively modest clutch size and single annual breeding event are consistent with a broader bowerbird pattern of low fecundity and extended parental care, although bower-building behavior in this genus is absent. Population densities vary locally in response to fruit abundance, and the species appears to undertake altitudinal movements in some parts of its range to track seasonal fruiting peaks, demonstrating a flexible spatial ecology that buffers against resource unpredictability in its montane and lowland habitats.
